title: Two Sum
description:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices** of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Every input has exactly one valid answer, and you can't use the same element twice. You can return the two indices in any order.

examples.explanation: nums[0] + nums[1] == 9, so we return [0, 1].

hints: For each number `x`, what *other* number would you need to complete the pair? Is there a fast way to check whether you've already seen it?
A hash map from value → index lets you look up the 'complement' (`target - x`) in O(1) time.
Loop once with `enumerate`. If `target - x` is already in your map, return `[map[target - x], i]`. Otherwise store `map[x] = i` and keep going.

title: Contains Duplicate
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `True` if **any value appears at least twice**, and `False` if every element is distinct.

examples.explanation: The value 1 shows up at index 0 and index 3.

hints: If the array were sorted, where would two equal values end up relative to each other?
A `set` remembers everything you've seen, with O(1) membership checks.
Loop over `nums`: if `x` is already in your set, return `True`; otherwise add it. If the loop finishes, return `False`. (One-liner: `len(set(nums)) < len(nums)`.)

title: Valid Anagram
description:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `True` if `t` is an **anagram** of `s`, and `False` otherwise.

An anagram uses exactly the same letters as the original, the same number of times, just rearranged.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Two words are anagrams exactly when every letter appears the same number of times in both.
Count characters with a dictionary (or `collections.Counter`), or compare the sorted strings.
Quick exit if `len(s) != len(t)`. Then build letter counts for both strings and check they're equal: `Counter(s) == Counter(t)`.

title: Group Anagrams
description:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group the **anagrams** together. You can return the groups in any order, and the words inside each group in any order.

Two strings are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the other's letters.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: What could you compute from a word that is *identical* for all of its anagrams?
Use that 'signature' as a dictionary key — either the sorted word, or a tuple of 26 letter counts.
Make `groups = defaultdict(list)`. For each word, `groups[tuple(sorted(word))].append(word)`. Return `list(groups.values())`.
complexity: O(n · k) time where k is the max word length, O(n · k) space

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` **most frequent** elements. You may return them in any order.

The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

*Follow-up:* can you beat O(n log n)?
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of distinct elements]
hints: Step one: figure out how many times each number appears.
Once you have counts, you want the k biggest. Sorting works; a heap does it in O(n log k); 'bucket sort' by frequency does it in O(n).
Bucket sort: `buckets[f]` = list of numbers that appear exactly `f` times (f goes up to `len(nums)`). Walk the buckets from the highest f downward, collecting numbers until you have k.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
description:
Design an algorithm that **encodes** a list of strings into a single string, and **decodes** that single string back into the original list.

Implement `encode(strs)` and `decode(s)` so that `decode(encode(strs)) == strs` for *any* list of strings. Watch out: the strings can contain any characters at all, including whatever delimiter you might be tempted to use!

The test runner calls `encode`, checks it returns a `str`, then passes that string to `decode` and compares the result with the original list.
constraints: strs[i] can contain any of the 256 ASCII characters.
hints: Joining with a separator like `,` breaks as soon as a string contains a `,`. How can the decoder know where each string ends *without* looking at its contents?
Store each string's length in front of it, followed by a marker character — e.g. `"4#neet"`.

encode: `''.join(f'{len(s)}#{s}' for s in strs)`. decode: keep an index `i`; scan forward to the next `#` to read the length L, take the next L characters as one string, jump `i` past them, and repeat until the end.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of **every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`**.

Your algorithm must run in O(n) time and **must not use division**.

*Follow-up:* can you do it with O(1) extra space (the output array doesn't count)?
constraints: Every prefix/suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: `answer[i]` = (product of everything to the *left* of i) × (product of everything to the *right* of i).
You can compute all the left-products in one pass, and all the right-products in another pass.
Fill `answer[i]` with the running prefix product going left→right. Then sweep right→left with a running `suffix` variable, multiplying `answer[i] *= suffix` and then `suffix *= nums[i]`.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description:
Given an **unsorted** array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values (like `4, 5, 6, 7`). The values don't need to be next to each other in the array.

Aim for an O(n) solution.

examples.explanation: The longest consecutive run is [1, 2, 3, 4], so the answer is 4.

hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). To get O(n), put everything in a `set` so you can ask "is x+1 here?" instantly.
Only start counting from numbers that *begin* a run — that is, `x` where `x - 1` is not in the set.
For each `x` in the set with `x - 1` not in the set, count upward `x+1, x+2, …` while they're in the set. Track the max length. Each number is visited at most twice overall.

title: Valid Palindrome
description:
A phrase is a **palindrome** if, after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing every non-alphanumeric character, it reads the same forward and backward. (Letters and digits count as alphanumeric.)

Given a string `s`, return `True` if it's a palindrome, or `False` otherwise.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: Cleaned up, it's "amanaplanacanalpanama" — a palindrome!
After cleaning, s is an empty string, which reads the same both ways.

constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters.
hints: The simple way: build a cleaned, lowercased string and compare it to its reverse. Can you do it without the extra string?
Use two pointers, one at each end, walking toward each other. `str.isalnum()` tells you which characters to skip.
While `l < r`: move `l` right past non-alphanumerics, move `r` left past non-alphanumerics, then compare `s[l].lower()` with `s[r].lower()`. Mismatch → `False`. Otherwise step both inward.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

title: 3Sum
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return **all unique triplets** `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` where `i`, `j`, `k` are different indices and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

The answer must not contain duplicate triplets. Order of triplets (and of numbers within a triplet) doesn't matter.

examples.explanation: No three numbers add up to 0.

hints: Sorting first makes both 'searching for a sum' and 'skipping duplicates' much easier.
Fix the first number `nums[i]`, then the problem becomes Two Sum on the rest of a *sorted* array — which two pointers solve in O(n).

Sort. For each `i` (skip if `nums[i] == nums[i-1]`), set `l = i+1, r = n-1`. If the sum is too small move `l` right, too big move `r` left; on a hit, record it, then move `l` right past any duplicates.
complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space (besides sorting)

title: Container With Most Water
description:
You're given an array `height` of length `n`. Picture `n` vertical lines, where line `i` goes from `(i, 0)` up to `(i, height[i])`.

Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container. Return the **maximum amount of water** a container can hold. (The container can't be tilted, so the water level is set by the shorter line.)

examples.explanation: Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7): width 7 × height 7 = 49.

hints: Area = `(r - l) * min(height[l], height[r])`. Checking every pair is O(n²) — can you rule pairs out?
Start with the widest container (both ends). Moving the *taller* line inward can never help — the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the shorter line.
Two pointers `l = 0`, `r = n-1`. Record the area, then move whichever pointer points to the shorter line inward. Repeat while `l < r`, keeping the max.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description:
You're given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`.

You want to buy on one day and sell on a **later** day. Return the maximum profit you can make. If no profit is possible, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 1 (price 1) and sell on day 4 (price 6): profit 6 − 1 = 5.
Prices only go down, so the best move is not to trade.

hints: If you sell on day i, which buy day gives you the best profit?
As you walk through the days, keep track of the cheapest price seen *so far*.
One pass: `lowest = min(lowest, price)` and `best = max(best, price - lowest)`. Return `best`.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description:
Given a string `s`, find the length of the **longest substring** that has no repeated characters.

A substring is a contiguous block of characters.

examples.explanation: "abc" has length 3.
"wke" works. Note "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
hints: Think of a window `s[l:r+1]` that never contains a duplicate. As `r` moves right, when does `l` need to move?
When the new character `s[r]` is already in the window, shrink from the left until it isn't. A set (or a dict of last-seen indices) tracks what's in the window.
With a dict `last[ch] = index`: for each `r`, if `s[r]` was seen at index ≥ `l`, jump `l = last[s[r]] + 1`. Then `last[s[r]] = r` and `best = max(best, r - l + 1)`.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description:
You're given a string `s` of uppercase letters and an integer `k`. You may pick any character and change it to any other uppercase letter — at most `k` times total.

Return the length of the **longest substring containing only one repeated letter** you can get after making those changes.

examples.explanation: Change both A's to B (or both B's to A) to get "BBBB".
Change the middle A to B: "AABBBBA" contains "BBBB".

constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters.
hints: For a given window, how many characters would you need to change so they all match? (Hint: keep the most common letter and change the rest.)
A window is valid when `window_length - count_of_most_frequent_letter <= k`. Grow the window to the right; shrink from the left when it becomes invalid.

Keep `count` of letters in the window and `maxf` = highest count seen. For each `r`: add `s[r]`, update `maxf`; while `(r - l + 1) - maxf > k`, remove `s[l]` and `l += 1`. Track the best window size. (It's fine that `maxf` never decreases!)

title: Minimum Window Substring
description:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the **shortest substring of `s`** that contains every character of `t` (including duplicates — if `t` has two `a`s, the window needs at least two `a`s).

If there's no such window, return the empty string `""`. If several windows tie for shortest, any one is accepted.

examples.explanation: "BANC" has an A, a B and a C, and nothing shorter does.
t needs two a's but s only has one.

constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
hints: Expand a window to the right until it contains everything in `t`, then try shrinking it from the left as much as possible while it stays valid.
Keep `need = Counter(t)` and a `window` counter. Track how many distinct characters currently meet their required count (`have` vs `required = len(need)`) so validity is an O(1) check.

For each `r`: add `s[r]`; if its count just reached `need[s[r]]`, `have += 1`. While `have == required`: record the window if it's the smallest yet, then remove `s[l]` (if its count drops below `need`, `have -= 1`) and `l += 1`.

title: Valid Parentheses
description:
Given a string `s` made of just the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, decide whether it's **valid**:

1. Every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket.
2. Brackets close in the correct order.
3. Every closing bracket has a matching opening bracket.
constraints: s consists only of the characters '()[]{}'.
hints: When you see a closing bracket, which opening bracket does it need to match?
The most recent *unmatched* opening bracket — last in, first out. That's a stack!
Push opening brackets. On a closing bracket, if the stack is empty or its top isn't the matching opener, return `False`; otherwise pop. At the end, the string is valid only if the stack is empty.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
An array of **unique** integers was sorted in ascending order and then **rotated** some number of times. For example, `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` rotated 4 times becomes `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`.

Given the rotated array `nums`, return its minimum element. Your algorithm must run in **O(log n)** time.

examples.explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5], rotated 3 times.

constraints: nums is sorted and rotated 1 to n times.
hints: O(log n) means binary search. Compare the middle element to something that tells you which half the 'drop' is in.
Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[r]`. If `nums[mid] > nums[r]`, the minimum must be to the right of `mid`. Otherwise it's at `mid` or to its left.
`l, r = 0, n-1`. While `l < r`: `mid = (l + r) // 2`; if `nums[mid] > nums[r]`: `l = mid + 1` else `r = mid`. Return `nums[l]`.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
An ascending array of **distinct** integers has been rotated at some unknown pivot (for example `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`).

Given the rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it isn't there. You must write an **O(log n)** algorithm.
constraints: All values in nums are unique.
hints: When you split a rotated array at `mid`, at least one of the two halves is perfectly sorted.
Figure out which half is sorted (compare `nums[l]` with `nums[mid]`), then check whether `target` falls inside that sorted half's range.

If `nums[l] <= nums[mid]` (left half sorted): if `nums[l] <= target < nums[mid]` search left (`r = mid - 1`), else search right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: if `nums[mid] < target <= nums[r]` go right, else go left.

title: Reverse Linked List
description:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the **new head**.

(In the examples, linked lists are written as arrays — the test runner builds real `ListNode` chains for you.)

#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

hints: Walk the list once, flipping each node's `next` pointer to point backward. What do you need to remember so you don't lose the rest of the list?
Keep two pointers: `prev` (starts as `None`) and `cur` (starts at `head`). Save `cur.next` before you overwrite it.
Loop while `cur`: `nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt`. When the loop ends, `prev` is the new head.
solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        prev, cur = None, head
        while cur:
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = prev
            prev, cur = cur, nxt
        return prev

description:

Merge them into one sorted list by splicing together the nodes of the two lists, and return the head of the merged list.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each list <= 50

solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:

#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]

        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        while heap:
            _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
            tail.next = tail = node
            if node.next:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
        return dummy.next

# Definition for a binary tree node.

#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []
        queue = deque([root] if root else [])
        while queue:
            level = []
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                node = queue.popleft()
                level.append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right:
                    queue.append(node.right)
            result.append(level)
        return result

                cur = cur.left
            cur = stack.pop()
            k -= 1
            if k == 0:
                return cur.val
            cur = cur.right

# Definition for a binary tree node.

#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, preorder: List[int], inorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
        pos = 0

        def build(lo, hi):
            nonlocal pos
            if lo > hi:
                return None
            val = preorder[pos]
            pos += 1
            node = TreeNode(val)
            mid = index[val]
            node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
            node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
            return node

        return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

            right = max(dfs(node.right), 0)

        return best

hints: Keeping one sorted list makes `addNum` O(n). The median only depends on the middle — what if you split the numbers into a 'small half' and a 'large half'?

Use two heaps: a **max-heap** for the smaller half and a **min-heap** for the larger half. Keep their sizes within 1 of each other. (Python's `heapq` is a min-heap — store negatives for the max-heap.)

addNum: push `-num` onto `small`; then move the largest of `small` over to `large` (`heappush(large, -heappop(small))`); if `large` gets bigger than `small`, move its smallest back. findMedian: if `small` is bigger return `-small[0]`, else return `(-small[0] + large[0]) / 2`.
driver:
def drive(args):
    return run_design(MedianFinder, args[0], args[1])

title: Combination Sum
description:
Given an array of **distinct** integers `candidates` and a `target`, return all **unique combinations** of candidates that add up to `target`. You may return them in any order.

The same number may be chosen **any number of times**. Two combinations are different if the count of at least one number differs.

examples.explanation: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 (2 used twice), and 7 = 7.

hints: Think of building a combination one choice at a time, and 'undoing' choices to explore alternatives — that's backtracking.
To avoid duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2], only ever pick candidates at the current index or later. At each step you can either reuse `candidates[i]` again, or move on to `i + 1`.

`dfs(i, path, total)`: if `total == target`, record `path[:]`; if `i == len(candidates)` or `total > target`, return. Otherwise: append `candidates[i]`, recurse with the **same** `i`; pop it; then recurse with `i + 1`.

title: Word Search
description:
Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and a string `word`, return `True` if `word` exists in the grid.

The word must be built from letters of sequentially **adjacent** cells (horizontally or vertically). The same cell can't be used more than once.

examples.explanation: You'd need to reuse the B cell.

constraints: board and word contain only English letters.
hints: Try starting from every cell. From a cell, the next letter of the word must be in one of its 4 neighbors.
Use DFS with backtracking: mark a cell as 'in use' while exploring from it, and un-mark it when you return so other paths can use it.

`dfs(r, c, i)`: if `i == len(word)` return `True`; if out of bounds, or `board[r][c] != word[i]`, return `False`. Temporarily set `board[r][c] = '#'`, try the 4 neighbors with `i + 1`, restore the letter, and return whether any worked.

title: Number of Islands
description:
Given an `m x n` grid where `"1"` is land and `"0"` is water, return the **number of islands**.

An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically, surrounded by water. Assume everything outside the grid is water.
hints: Scan the grid. Whenever you find land you haven't explored yet, you've discovered a new island.
When you discover an island, 'sink' (or mark as visited) every land cell connected to it with DFS or BFS, so you don't count it again.
Loop over every cell; if it's `"1"`, increment the count and run `dfs(r, c)`, which sets the cell to `"0"` and recurses into its 4 neighbors that are in bounds and `"1"`.
complexity: O(m · n) time, O(m · n) worst-case space

title: Clone Graph
description:
You're given a reference to one node of a **connected, undirected graph**. Return a **deep copy** (clone) of the graph: brand new nodes with the same values and the same connections.

Each node has a `val` (an int) and `neighbors` (a list of nodes). In the tests, node values are `1..n` and the graph is written as an adjacency list: `adjList[i]` lists the neighbors of the node with value `i + 1`. You're given the node with value 1.

The runner also checks that you didn't hand back any of the original nodes.

examples.explanation: A single node with no neighbors.
An empty graph — the input node is None.

constraints: No repeated edges or self-loops; the graph is connected.
starter:
# Definition for a Node.
# class Node:
#     def __init__(self, val = 0, neighbors = None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.neighbors = neighbors if neighbors is not None else []

class Solution:
    def cloneGraph(self, node: Optional['Node']) -> Optional['Node']:
        pass
hints: You need to visit every node (DFS or BFS) and create a copy of each one exactly once — even though the graph has cycles.
Keep a dictionary `old_node → new_node`. Before cloning a node, check whether it's already in there.

`def clone(n)`: if `n in copies` return `copies[n]`; make `copy = Node(n.val)`, store `copies[n] = copy` **before** recursing, then `copy.neighbors = [clone(nb) for nb in n.neighbors]` and return `copy`. Handle `node is None`.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description:
An `m x n` island borders the **Pacific Ocean** on its top and left edges, and the **Atlantic Ocean** on its bottom and right edges. `heights[r][c]` is the height of each cell.

Rain water flows from a cell to a neighboring cell (up/down/left/right) if the neighbor's height is **less than or equal to** the current height. Water flows from edge cells straight into the adjacent ocean.

Return a list of all coordinates `[r, c]` from which rain water can reach **both** oceans, in any order.
hints: Checking every cell separately is slow. Flip the question around: start from the *oceans* and see which cells water could have come from.
From the ocean edges, walk 'uphill' (to neighbors with height >= current). Do one search from all Pacific edge cells and another from all Atlantic edge cells.

Make sets `pac` and `atl`. DFS from every top-row and left-column cell into `pac`, and from every bottom-row and right-column cell into `atl`, only stepping to neighbors with `heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]`. Answer: cells in both sets.
solution:
class Solution:
    def pacificAtlantic(self, heights: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])

        def reach(starts):
            seen = set(starts)
            stack = list(starts)
            while stack:
                r, c = stack.pop()
                for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                    if (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and (nr, nc) not in seen
                            and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]):
                        seen.add((nr, nc))
                        stack.append((nr, nc))
            return seen

        pac = reach([(0, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)])
        atl = reach([(rows - 1, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, cols - 1) for r in range(rows)])
        return [[r, c] for r, c in pac & atl]

title: Course Schedule
description:
There are `numCourses` courses labeled `0` to `numCourses - 1`. `prerequisites[i] = [a, b]` means you must take course `b` **before** course `a`.

Return `True` if it's possible to finish every course, otherwise `False`.

examples.explanation: Take course 0, then course 1.
Each course needs the other first — a cycle!

hints: Model courses as a directed graph (an edge from prerequisite → course). When is it *impossible* to finish?
It's impossible exactly when the graph has a **cycle**. Detect one with DFS (track nodes on the current path) or with Kahn's topological sort.

Kahn's algorithm: count each course's incoming edges (`indegree`). Put all courses with indegree 0 in a queue; pop one, count it as taken, and decrement the indegree of courses that depend on it, enqueuing any that reach 0. Return `taken == numCourses`.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
description:
You have a graph of `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1`, and a list `edges` where `edges[i] = [a, b]` is an undirected edge between `a` and `b`.

Return the number of **connected components** in the graph.
hints: Each component is a group of nodes you can reach from one another. You could DFS from every unvisited node and count how many times you start a new search.
Union-Find (disjoint set) is also great: start with n separate groups, and every edge that joins two *different* groups reduces the count by one.
`parent = list(range(n))`. `find(x)` follows parents to the root (with path compression). For each edge, if `find(a) != find(b)`, link one root to the other and do `n -= 1`. Return `n`.

title: Graph Valid Tree
description:
You have `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of undirected `edges`.

Return `True` if these edges form a **valid tree**: every node is connected, and there are no cycles.

examples.explanation: 1 → 2 → 3 → 1 is a cycle.

hints: A tree with n nodes always has exactly n − 1 edges. Is that enough on its own?
With exactly n − 1 edges, the graph is a tree if and only if it's connected (or, equivalently, has no cycle).

Return `False` if `len(edges) != n - 1`. Otherwise, DFS/BFS from node 0 and check that you visit all n nodes — or use Union-Find and return `False` if any edge connects two nodes already in the same set.

title: Alien Dictionary
description:
An alien language uses lowercase English letters, but in an unknown **order**.

You're given a list of `words` from the alien dictionary, **sorted** by the rules of that language. Return a string of the language's unique letters in a valid order. If no order is consistent with the list, return `""`. If several orders work, return any of them.

Ordering rules: comparing two words, the first position where they differ decides the order. If there's no difference in the shorter length, the shorter word comes first — so `"abc"` before `"ab"` is invalid.

examples.explanation: z < x and x < z can't both be true.
A word can't come before its own prefix.

hints: Comparing each pair of *adjacent* words gives you at most one fact: the first differing letters `a`, `b` mean `a` comes before `b`.
Those facts form a directed graph of letters. A valid alphabet is a topological ordering of that graph; a cycle means there's no answer. Don't forget the prefix rule!

Add every letter as a node. For each adjacent pair, find the first differing letters and add edge `a → b` (if `w1` is longer and `w2` is its prefix, return `""`). Then run Kahn's algorithm; if you can't output every letter, return `""`.
complexity: O(total characters) time, O(1) space (≤ 26 letters)

title: Climbing Stairs
description:
You're climbing a staircase with `n` steps. Each move, you can climb either **1 or 2** steps.

How many distinct ways can you reach the top?
hints: Think about your very last move onto step n. Where could you have been just before it?
You arrived from step n−1 (a 1-step) or step n−2 (a 2-step), so `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)`. Look familiar? 🐇
Bottom-up with two variables: `a, b = 1, 1` (ways to reach steps 0 and 1). Repeat `n - 1` times: `a, b = b, a + b`. Return `b`. (Plain recursion without memoization is too slow!)

title: House Robber
description:
You're a (very polite) robber planning to rob houses along a street. `nums[i]` is the money in house `i`.

The catch: **adjacent houses have connected alarms**, so you can't rob two houses next to each other on the same night. Return the most money you can collect.

examples.explanation: Rob house 0 (1) and house 2 (3).
Rob houses 0, 2 and 4: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.

hints: At each house you have two choices: rob it, or skip it. What does each choice force on its neighbor?
Let `best(i)` = max money from houses `0..i`. Then `best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i])`.
Keep two running values: `prev2` (best up to i−2) and `prev1` (best up to i−1). For each `x`: `prev2, prev1 = prev1, max(prev1, prev2 + x)`. Return `prev1`.

title: House Robber II
description:
Same polite robber, new street: this time the houses are arranged in a **circle**, so the first house and the last house are neighbors.

Adjacent houses still can't both be robbed. Given `nums`, return the most money you can collect.

examples.explanation: Houses 0 and 2 are neighbors now, so the best is just house 1.

hints: The circle only adds one extra rule: you can't rob both the first and the last house.
So either you skip the first house, or you skip the last house. Each of those cases is a straight line — the original House Robber!
Write a helper for the line version. Return `max(nums[0], helper(nums[1:]), helper(nums[:-1]))` — the `nums[0]` handles a single house.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description:
Given a string `s`, return the **longest substring** of `s` that is a palindrome (reads the same forwards and backwards).

If there are several of the same maximum length, any of them is accepted.

examples.explanation: "aba" is also a valid answer.

constraints: s consists of digits and English letters.
hints: Every palindrome has a center. Instead of checking every substring, what if you grew outward from each possible center?
There are 2n − 1 centers: each character (odd-length palindromes) and each gap between two characters (even-length ones).
For each `i`, expand with `l, r = i, i` and again with `l, r = i, i + 1`: while `l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]`, step outward. Track the longest `s[l+1:r]` found.

title: Palindromic Substrings
description:
Given a string `s`, return **how many of its substrings are palindromes**.

Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same letters.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: This is a close cousin of 'Longest Palindromic Substring'. Can you reuse the expand-around-center idea?
Every time an expansion step succeeds (`s[l] == s[r]`), you've found one more palindrome.
For each of the 2n − 1 centers, expand outward while the ends match, adding 1 to the count for each successful step.

title: Decode Ways
description:
A secret message of letters was encoded as digits using `"A" → "1"`, `"B" → "2"`, …, `"Z" → "26"`.

Given a string of digits `s`, return the **number of ways to decode it** back into letters. Codes like `"06"` are invalid (no leading zeros), so a `0` must be part of `10` or `20`. If there's no valid decoding, return `0`.

examples.explanation: "06" can't be decoded — 6 is "6", not "06".

constraints: s contains only digits and may have leading zeros.
hints: Read the string left to right. At each spot, you can decode either one digit or two digits. Which choices are allowed?
One digit works if it isn't `'0'`. Two digits work if they form a number from 10 to 26. Let `ways(i)` = number of ways to decode `s[:i]`.
`dp[0] = 1`. For `i` from 1 to n: if `s[i-1] != '0'`, `dp[i] += dp[i-1]`; if `i >= 2` and `10 <= int(s[i-2:i]) <= 26`, `dp[i] += dp[i-2]`. Return `dp[n]` (you can shrink it to two variables).

title: Coin Change
description:
You're given coin denominations `coins` and a total `amount`. You have an unlimited supply of each coin.

Return the **fewest coins** needed to make exactly `amount`. If it can't be done, return `-1`.
hints: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails — try coins `[1, 3, 4]` with amount 6. Think about the smallest *sub-amounts* instead.
Let `dp[a]` = fewest coins to make amount `a`. If the last coin used is `c`, then `dp[a] = 1 + dp[a - c]`.
`dp = [0] + [inf] * amount`. For `a` from 1 to amount, for each coin `c <= a`: `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)`. Return `dp[amount]` if it's finite, else -1.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the **contiguous subarray** with the largest product, and return that product.

examples.explanation: [2, 3] has product 6.

constraints: Every subarray product fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Unlike sums, a very *negative* product can flip into the very best one when multiplied by another negative.
Track both the largest **and** the smallest product of a subarray ending at each position.
For each `x`: `candidates = (x, x * hi, x * lo)`; `hi, lo = max(candidates), min(candidates)`; `best = max(best, hi)`. Start with `hi = lo = best = nums[0]`.

title: Word Break
description:
Given a string `s` and a list of words `wordDict`, return `True` if `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more dictionary words (separated by spaces).

Dictionary words may be reused any number of times.

examples.explanation: "apple pen apple" — reusing "apple" is fine.

hints: If `s` starts with a dictionary word `w`, then the question becomes: can the *rest* of `s` be broken? That repeats a lot of work — remember the answers.
Let `dp[i]` = `True` if the prefix `s[:i]` can be segmented. `dp[0] = True` (the empty string).
For `i` from 1 to `len(s)`, for each word `w`: if `i >= len(w)` and `dp[i - len(w)]` and `s[i - len(w):i] == w`, set `dp[i] = True`. Return `dp[len(s)]`.
complexity: O(n · m · k) time (m words, k max length), O(n) space

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest **strictly increasing subsequence**.

A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements — e.g. `[3, 6, 2, 7]` is a subsequence of `[0, 3, 1, 6, 2, 2, 7]`.

*Follow-up:* can you do it in O(n log n)?

examples.explanation: [2, 3, 7, 101] is one longest option.

hints: Let `dp[i]` = length of the longest increasing subsequence that *ends* at index `i`. How does it relate to earlier entries?
`dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j])` over all `j < i` with `nums[j] < nums[i]` (or just 1). That's O(n²) and totally fine here.

O(n log n) bonus: keep `tails`, where `tails[k]` is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each `x`, find `i = bisect_left(tails, x)`; replace `tails[i]` with `x` (or append if `i == len(tails)`). Answer: `len(tails)`.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Unique Paths
description:
A robot sits in the top-left corner of an `m x n` grid. It can only move **right** or **down**, one cell at a time.

How many different paths can it take to reach the bottom-right corner?

examples.explanation: Right→Down→Down, Down→Down→Right, Down→Right→Down.

hints: To arrive at a cell, the robot must have come from the cell above it or the cell to its left.
`paths(r, c) = paths(r-1, c) + paths(r, c-1)`, and every cell in the top row or left column has exactly 1 path.
Keep a single row `row = [1] * n`. Repeat `m - 1` times: for `c` in `1..n-1`, `row[c] += row[c - 1]`. Return `row[-1]`. (Math shortcut: `comb(m + n - 2, m - 1)`.)

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their **longest common subsequence** (or `0` if they share none).

A subsequence keeps the characters' order but can skip some — `"ace"` is a subsequence of `"abcde"`.

examples.explanation: "ace" is in both.

hints: Compare the strings from the front (or back). If the first characters match, great — what then? If they don't, which character could you drop?
Let `dp[i][j]` = LCS of `text1[i:]` and `text2[j:]`. If `text1[i] == text2[j]`: `1 + dp[i+1][j+1]`. Otherwise: `max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j+1])`.
Make a `(len1 + 1) x (len2 + 1)` table of zeros and fill it from the bottom-right corner backward using that rule. The answer is `dp[0][0]`.

title: Maximum Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the **contiguous subarray** (with at least one number) that has the largest sum, and return that sum.
hints: Walk left to right, keeping a running sum. When would carrying the running sum forward *hurt* you?
If the running sum ever goes negative, it can only drag down whatever comes next — so start fresh. (This is Kadane's algorithm.)
`cur = 0; best = nums[0]`. For each `x`: `cur = max(cur, 0) + x` (drop a negative prefix), then `best = max(best, cur)`. Return `best`.

title: Jump Game
description:
You start at index 0 of the array `nums`. Each value `nums[i]` is the **maximum** jump length from that position (you can jump any distance from 0 up to it).

Return `True` if you can reach the last index, otherwise `False`.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step to index 1, then 3 steps to the end.
Every route lands on index 3, whose jump length is 0.

hints: You don't need to know *how* to get somewhere — only the farthest index you can possibly reach so far.
Walk forward keeping `reach`, the farthest reachable index. If you ever stand on an index greater than `reach`, you're stuck.

For each `i`: if `i > reach` return `False`; otherwise `reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])`. Return `True` at the end. (Or go backward: move a 'goal' left whenever `i + nums[i] >= goal`, and check if goal hits 0.)

title: Insert Interval
description:
You're given a list of **non-overlapping** intervals `intervals`, sorted by start, and one more interval `newInterval = [start, end]`.

Insert `newInterval` so that the list stays sorted and non-overlapping (merge overlaps where needed), and return the result.
constraints: intervals is sorted by start and has no overlaps.
hints: Every existing interval falls into one of three groups: completely before the new one, overlapping it, or completely after it.
Intervals ending before `newInterval` starts go straight into the result. Overlapping ones get merged into `newInterval` by widening it. Then everything after.

Loop: if `cur[1] < new[0]` append `cur`; elif `cur[0] > new[1]` append `new`, then set `new = cur` (the leftover gets appended at the end); else `new = [min(new[0], cur[0]), max(new[1], cur[1])]`. Finally append `new`.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output

title: Merge Intervals
description:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, **merge all overlapping intervals** and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges.

Intervals that just touch (like `[1,4]` and `[4,5]`) count as overlapping.
hints: Overlaps are hard to spot in a random order. What order would put overlapping intervals right next to each other?
Sort by start time. Now each interval either overlaps the *last* merged interval, or starts a new one.
Sort, then for each `[s, e]`: if `result` is non-empty and `s <= result[-1][1]`, set `result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], e)`; otherwise append `[s, e]`.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description:
Given an array of `intervals`, return the **minimum number of intervals you need to remove** so that the rest don't overlap.

Intervals that only touch at a point (like `[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) do **not** overlap.

examples.explanation: Remove [1,3] and the rest are fine.

hints: Flip the question: what's the *maximum* number of intervals you can keep without any overlaps?
Greedy: when two intervals clash, keep the one that **ends earlier** — it leaves the most room for everything after it.
Sort by end time. Track `end` of the last kept interval (start at `-inf`). For each interval: if `start >= end`, keep it (`end = its end`); otherwise count it as removed.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Meeting Rooms
description:
Given an array of meeting time `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, decide whether one person could attend **all** the meetings.

A meeting ending at time `t` and another starting at time `t` don't conflict.

examples.explanation: [0,30] overlaps both other meetings.

hints: If you lined the meetings up in the order they happen, where would a conflict show up?
After sorting by start time, a conflict can only happen between *neighboring* meetings.
Sort by start. For each `i >= 1`, if `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]` return `False`. Otherwise return `True`.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Meeting Rooms II
description:
Given an array of meeting time `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, return the **minimum number of conference rooms** needed so every meeting has a room.

A room freed at time `t` can be used by a meeting starting at time `t`.
hints: The answer is the largest number of meetings happening at the same moment.
Sweep through time: every start needs a room and every end frees one. Sort the start times and end times separately.

Sort `starts` and `ends`. Walk through `starts` with pointer `s` and keep pointer `e` into `ends`: if `starts[s] < ends[e]`, a new room is needed (`rooms += 1`); otherwise a room frees up (`e += 1`). Track the max. (A min-heap of end times also works.)
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Rotate Image
description:
You're given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate it **90 degrees clockwise**, **in place** — modify the input matrix directly instead of creating a new one.

Your function returns nothing; the runner checks the matrix you modified.
hints: A 90° rotation can be built from two simpler flips you can each do in place.
Try: transpose the matrix (swap `matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]`), then reverse each row. Check it on a 3×3 by hand!
Transpose: for `i` in range(n), for `j` in range(i + 1, n), swap `matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i]`. Then `for row in matrix: row.reverse()`.
driver:
def drive(args):
    matrix = args[0]
    Solution().rotate(matrix)
    return matrix

title: Spiral Matrix
description: Given an `m x n` `matrix`, return all of its elements in **spiral order**: across the top row, down the right side, back along the bottom, up the left side, and then spiral inward.
hints: Keep track of four boundaries — `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` — that shrink as you peel off each layer.
Each loop: walk the top row left→right (then `top += 1`), the right column top→bottom (`right -= 1`), the bottom row right→left (`bottom -= 1`), the left column bottom→top (`left += 1`).
Careful with single rows/columns: before walking the bottom row check `top <= bottom`, and before walking the left column check `left <= right`. Loop while `top <= bottom and left <= right`.
complexity: O(m · n) time, O(1) extra space

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description:
Given an `m x n` integer `matrix`, if an element is `0`, set its **entire row and column** to `0`. Do it **in place**.

*Follow-up:* the easy version uses O(m + n) extra space. Can you get it down to O(1)?
hints: If you zero things out as soon as you see a 0, the new zeros will trick you into wiping out extra rows and columns. Find all of them first.
First pass: record which rows and which columns contain a zero (two sets). Second pass: zero every cell whose row or column was recorded.

O(1)-space trick: use the first row and first column themselves as the 'recorded' markers, plus one extra flag for whether the first row itself needs zeroing. Fill the inner cells first, then the first column/row last.
complexity: O(m · n) time, O(m + n) space (O(1) with the marker trick)
driver:
def drive(args):
    matrix = args[0]
    Solution().setZeroes(matrix)
    return matrix

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Given a positive integer `n`, return the number of `1` bits in its binary representation (also called its **Hamming weight**).

examples.explanation: 11 in binary is 1011 — three 1s.

hints: You can look at the lowest bit with `n & 1`, and drop it with `n >> 1`.
Loop until `n` becomes 0, adding `n & 1` to a counter and shifting right each time.
Neat trick: `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit. Count how many times you can do `n &= n - 1` before `n` hits 0. (Python cheat: `bin(n).count('1')` — but try the bit way!)
complexity: O(number of set bits) time, O(1) space

title: Counting Bits
description:
Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` where `ans[i]` is the **number of 1 bits** in the binary form of `i`, for every `i` from `0` to `n`.

*Follow-up:* can you do it in O(n) — one pass, without counting each number's bits from scratch?
hints: Look for a relationship between `i` and a smaller number whose answer you already computed.
`i >> 1` is `i` with its last bit removed, and it's smaller than `i`. The only difference is that last bit, `i & 1`.
`ans = [0] * (n + 1)`; for `i` in `1..n`: `ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`. Return `ans`.

title: Reverse Bits
description:
Reverse the bits of a **32-bit unsigned integer** `n` and return the result as an integer.

For example, bit 0 (the lowest) becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. Always treat the number as exactly 32 bits, including leading zeros.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2^32 - 1 (passed as a regular Python int)
hints: Build the answer one bit at a time: take bits off the low end of `n` and push them onto the low end of the result.
Each step: shift the result left by 1 to make room, then OR in `n & 1`. Then shift `n` right by 1.
`result = 0`; repeat exactly 32 times: `result = (result << 1) | (n & 1)`; `n >>= 1`. Return `result`. (Exactly 32 iterations matters — leading zeros count!)

title: Missing Number
description:
You're given an array `nums` containing `n` **distinct** numbers taken from the range `[0, n]`. Exactly one number in that range is missing — return it.

*Follow-up:* can you do it with O(1) extra space and O(n) time?

examples.explanation: n = 3, so the range is 0..3, and 2 is missing.

constraints: All numbers are unique and in [0, n].
hints: You know exactly which numbers *should* be there: 0, 1, …, n.
Math way: the sum of 0..n is `n * (n + 1) // 2`. Bit way: `x ^ x == 0`, so XOR-ing every index with every value cancels out all the pairs.
`return n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(nums)` — or start `res = n` and do `res ^= i ^ nums[i]` for every `i`; what's left is the missing number.

title: Sum of Two Integers
description:
Given two integers `a` and `b`, return their sum **without using the `+` or `-` operators**.

(The runner can't stop you from using `+`… but the whole point is the bit trick. 😉 Heads up: Python ints have unlimited size, so negative numbers need a 32-bit mask.)
hints: When you add in binary, each column produces a 'sum bit' and a 'carry bit'. Which bitwise operators compute those?
`a ^ b` adds without carrying. `(a & b) << 1` is the carry. Keep adding the carry back in until there is none.

Python needs a 32-bit mask: `mask = 0xFFFFFFFF`. Loop while `b`: `a, b = (a ^ b) & mask, ((a & b) << 1) & mask`. At the end, if `a > 0x7FFFFFFF` it's negative: return `~(a ^ mask)`; otherwise return `a`.
